title: Anamnestic Questionnaire for the Diagnostic Differentiation of Bilateral Vestibulopathy and Sensory Polyneuropathy in Sensory Ataxia: A Prospective Questionnaire-Based Study of the Diagnostic Accuracy of a Single Anamnestic Discriminator
summary:
Problems with walking, standing, and keeping balance are common reasons for people to see a neurologist. People may feel unsteady when they walk or stand, have trouble coordinating their movements, or struggle to maintain balance—especially during more demanding activities, such as walking on uneven ground, in the dark, or while moving quickly.
During a neurological examination, these difficulties may appear as  "ataxia", meaning impaired coordination of walking and standing. There are several possible causes. One is a problem in the cerebellum, the part of the brain that helps coordinate movement. Cerebellar disorders can often be recognised relatively easily during a clinical examination because they usually cause additional characteristic signs.
Another cause is called sensory ataxia. This occurs when the brain receives too little or unreliable information from body systems that are important for balance and posture. Two particularly important causes are:

-Bilateral vestibulopathy (BVP): reduced function of the balance organs in both inner ears.
- Sensory polyneuropathy (PNP):damage to peripheral nerves, particularly those that provide information about the position and movement of the legs and feet.

In later stages, these two conditions often show characteristic features that help distinguish them. Early in the course of disease, however, telling them apart can be difficult. People with either condition may report that they walk and stand less securely in the dark or on uneven surfaces. Common bedside tests, such as the Romberg test—standing still with the feet together and the eyes closed—also cannot always reliably distinguish between BVP and PNP. More specialised tests are often necessary. These may include tests of inner-ear balance function, such as the video head impulse test, or nerve tests that measure how quickly electrical signals travel through the nerves. Nerve conduction studies are commonly available and are often used to diagnose PNP. In contrast, specialised tests of vestibular function are not available in every neurological practice. As a result, BVP may sometimes remain undetected or be diagnosed late. However, the diagnostic assessment can be time-consuming and may require specialised equipment.

This study investigates whether a simple question from the medical history could help distinguish between BVP and PNP:

“Are you still able to ride a bicycle?”

A single, well-chosen question can sometimes be informative. For example, in Parkinson’s disease, the ability to cycle may remain preserved even when walking is severely affected. Asking about cycling can therefore help distinguish typical Parkinson’s disease from certain atypical parkinsonian disorders.
A similar principle may apply to BVP. Many people with BVP report major difficulties with cycling, and some are no longer able to cycle at all. This may be because cycling requires the body to maintain balance during continuous movement while also keeping vision stable. In BVP, the balance organs of both inner ears do not provide normal information, and vision can become blurred during rapid head movement. Although people may partly compensate for balance problems while walking—for example, by walking more slowly, taking wider steps, or relying more on vision—these strategies may work less well while cycling.
By contrast, people with PNP mainly have reduced information from the nerves in their feet and legs about body position and movement. Their ability to cycle may therefore be less affected than in people with BVP. However, this has not yet been studied systematically.

The aim of this study is to develop a short questionnaire that helps distinguish between two forms of sensory ataxia:

- Sensory ataxia mainly caused by impaired inner-ear balance function, i.e. BVP.
- Sensory ataxia mainly caused by impaired position sense due to PNP.

The central question is whether preserved cycling ability can serve as a useful indicator in this distinction. The questionnaire will also include additional questions about symptoms and everyday activities that may differ between BVP and PNP.
The questionnaire results will be compared with established clinical diagnostic tests. These include nerve conduction studies for PNP and internationally accepted diagnostic criteria and vestibular function tests for BVP.

Who will not participate
Some people have more than one cause of ataxia. For example, **CANVAS syndrome** is a rare, usually genetic disorder that may affect peripheral nerves, the balance organs of the inner ears, and the cerebellum at the same time. People with such mixed forms, as well as people whose ataxia is caused solely by a cerebellar disorder, will not be included in this questionnaire study.
conditions: Patients with bilateral vestibulopathy (BVP) and patients with sensory, proprioceptive polyneuropathy (PNP).

interventions.name: Following detailed study information, an adequate reflection period, and written informed consent, patients presenting to the Department of Neurology with sensory gait and stance ataxia (predominantly vestibular or proprioceptive) will be recruited. Patients will complete the questionnaire independe

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clinically established sensory gait and/or stance ataxia, predominantly vestibular (BVP) or predominantly proprioceptive (PNP), according to established diagnostic criteria  
Written informed consent, obtained following adequate study information  Availability of the instrumental neurophysiological examinations required to confirm the diagnosis, such as video head impulse testing (vHIT), caloric testing, and nerve conduction studies  
Sufficient proficiency in German  
Previous experience with riding a bicycle
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients unable to provide informed consent  
- Minor patients  
- Patients without sufficient German-language proficiency  
- Ataxia not predominantly sensory in origin, for example cerebellar ataxia or ataxia caused by other central nervous system or structural disorders  
- Patients without prior cycling experience, or patients unable to cycle for reasons unrelated to the condition under investigation
